crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: How a paper is cited covers the paths that connect one research work to another: direct references, in-text mentions, and the contexts in which a later paper uses an earlier one. It sits inside citation mapping and discovery, where the goal is to trace influence, find related work, and see how a claim travels from its source into new arguments. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Citation work runs on persistent identifiers, metadata records, and indexing services that store references and link them across versions. A DOI or another stable identifier points to a paper, while services such as Crossref, OpenAlex, and Semantic Scholar collect reference lists, author names, venues, and dates. Full-text sources, PDF parsers, and reference extraction tools turn a bibliography into structured edges between papers. The site's own library of 135 research papers and 12233 extracted claims sits on top of that layer, and its pages link to the original paper rather than to the Consensus search tool.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by extracting references from a paper, matching each reference to a canonical record, and recording the context around the citation. A reference parser reads the bibliography, a matching step resolves author, title, year, and venue against an index, and a context extractor captures the sentence or paragraph where the citation appears. Analysts then build a graph of nodes and edges, where nodes are papers and edges are citations, and they may weight edges by section, sentiment, or whether the citation is supportive, critical, or incidental. On this site, 12233 claims extracted from research works give a finer grain than a bare citation count, because a claim can be tied to the specific passage that cites it.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in citation mapping begin with copyright and database terms: reference lists may be factual, but full text, abstracts, and figures often carry restrictions. Provenance matters because a citation edge is only as good as the metadata behind it, and errors in author disambiguation, versioning, or venue names can create false links. Privacy and ethics also apply when citation graphs are used to evaluate people, since a citation is not a direct measure of quality or contribution. This site keeps provenance visible by linking to the original paper, not to the Consensus search tool, so a reader can inspect the source rather than trust a derived summary.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Citation mapping is moving toward richer context, open metadata, and better handling of preprints, datasets, and software as citable objects. Automated extraction and large language models can classify citation intent, but they also raise the risk of hallucinated references and silent errors, so verification against the original record remains central. Discovery systems are likely to combine citation graphs with semantic search, topic models, and claim-level indexes, which is why this site tracks 12233 claims alongside its 135 research papers. The direction is not just counting citations but showing how a specific idea moves through a literature and where it is reused, challenged, or left behind.
